title: Human activities which contribute to greenhouse gases

notes.definition: Some human activities increase the amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere: burning fossil fuels and deforestation increase carbon dioxide, and animal farming and landfill sites increase methane. Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe this will cause the Earth's surface temperature to rise and result in global climate change.
explanation: Human activities increase the amounts of two important greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide and methane. You need to recall two activities for each gas.

Carbon dioxide: (1) Burning fossil fuels (coal, crude oil products and natural gas) in power stations, vehicles, factories and homes. Combustion turns the carbon locked up in the fuel into carbon dioxide, for example CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). (2) Deforestation: cutting down and often burning forests. Burning releases carbon dioxide, and there are fewer trees to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.

Methane: (1) Animal farming: cattle and other livestock produce methane during digestion and release it. More people means more cattle are farmed. (2) Decomposition of rubbish in landfill sites: microorganisms break down waste without oxygen, releasing methane. Rice paddy fields are another source, because rice grows in waterlogged soil where decay happens without oxygen.

Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere to increase at the surface and that this will result in global climate change. Peer review means other scientists check the methods, data and conclusions before results are published, which reduces errors and bias and makes the findings more trustworthy.

However, it is difficult to model such complex systems as global climate change. The climate depends on many interacting factors, such as clouds, oceans, ice, living things and natural variation. This leads to simplified models, and to speculation and opinions in the media that may be based on only parts of the evidence and may be biased. When evaluating a report, ask: Is it peer reviewed? How big is the data set and over what time? Who funded or wrote it? Does it present all the evidence? Scientists also need to communicate their results clearly to a wide range of audiences, including the public and politicians, so that good decisions can be made.
keyFacts: Burning fossil fuels increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Deforestation increases carbon dioxide (burning trees, and less photosynthesis).
Decomposition of rubbish in landfill sites increases methane; rice paddy fields also release methane.
Many scientists, using peer-reviewed evidence, believe human activities will increase surface temperature and cause global climate change.
Climate is a complex system, so models are simplified and have uncertainties.
Media reports may be based on only part of the evidence and may be biased.

keyTerms.definition: Cutting down large areas of forest, often burning the trees, for land or timber.
A place where rubbish is buried; the waste decomposes without oxygen and releases methane.
Coal, crude oil or natural gas; burning these releases carbon dioxide.
The checking of scientific work by other experts in the same field before it is published.
A simplified representation, often a computer simulation, used to predict how a complex system such as the climate will change.
Presenting information in a one-sided way, for example by choosing only the evidence that supports a particular view.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think deforestation only matters because burning trees releases carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact it also matters because fewer trees remain to remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think methane comes mainly from burning fuels.
misconceptions.right: In fact burning methane produces carbon dioxide; human methane emissions come mainly from animal farming, landfill and rice fields (and leaks from gas extraction).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think anything reported in the media about climate change is scientific fact.
misconceptions.right: In fact media reports may be simplified, based on only parts of the evidence, or biased; peer-reviewed evidence is more reliable.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that because climate models are uncertain, they are worthless.
misconceptions.right: In fact models are simplified but still useful; many independent models and data sets agree that surface temperatures are rising.

realWorld: The Mauna Loa observatory in Hawaii has measured atmospheric carbon dioxide continuously since 1958, giving the rising curve shown in many textbooks.
Some landfill sites collect the methane they produce and burn it to generate electricity.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) summarises thousands of peer-reviewed studies for governments.
examTips: Learn two activities for each gas: carbon dioxide (burning fossil fuels, deforestation); methane (animal farming, landfill/decomposition of rubbish). Rice paddy fields is also accepted for methane.
For deforestation, give both reasons: burning releases carbon dioxide and fewer trees photosynthesise.
When evaluating evidence, comment on peer review, sample size and time span, who produced the report, and whether all the evidence is shown.
For percentage change always divide by the original (earlier) value.
summary: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels and deforestation.
Methane: animal farming and landfill sites (also rice paddy fields).
Peer-reviewed evidence suggests human activities will increase surface temperature and cause climate change.
Climate is complex, so models are simplified and uncertain.
Media reports may be speculative, selective or biased.
Peer review and clear communication to all audiences are important.

questions.question: Which human activity increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: burning fossil fuels
questions.explanation: Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Planting trees removes carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which human activity increases the amount of methane in the atmosphere?
markScheme: 1 mark: cattle farming
questions.explanation: Cattle release methane from digestion. The other options do not release methane.

questions.question: Rubbish decomposing in landfill sites releases which greenhouse gas?
markScheme: 1 mark: methane
questions.explanation: Microorganisms break down waste without oxygen, producing methane.

questions.question: What is meant by peer review?
options: A newspaper checks a scientist's spelling.
Scientists vote on whether they like a result.
The public decides if a theory is correct.
Other experts check scientific work before it is published.
markScheme: 1 mark: other experts check work before publication
questions.explanation: Peer review is checking by other scientists in the same field, which helps to find errors and bias.

questions.question: Why does deforestation increase carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Trees release carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Fewer trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, and burning the trees releases carbon dioxide.
Soil absorbs more carbon dioxide after trees are removed.
markScheme: 1 mark: fewer trees for photosynthesis and burning releases carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide; fewer trees means less removal. Burning adds carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which is the correct balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane?
markScheme: 1 mark: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
questions.explanation: 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side. The first is unbalanced; the third shows carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion) and is not balanced for oxygen.

questions.question: Why is it difficult to make accurate predictions about global climate change?
options: There are no greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
The climate is a complex system with many interacting factors, so models must be simplified.
markScheme: 1 mark: complex system, so models are simplified
questions.explanation: The climate involves oceans, clouds, ice, living things and natural variation, which are hard to model exactly.

questions.question: A newspaper article about climate change uses temperature data from one town for one year. What is the main weakness of this evidence?
options: The data set is too small and too short to show a global trend.
Temperatures cannot be measured in towns.
One year of data is too much information.
markScheme: 1 mark: data set too small/short to show a global trend
questions.explanation: Global climate change needs data from many places over many years; one town for one year may just show weather or natural variation.

questions.question: A report on climate change was paid for by an oil company and was not peer reviewed. Which is the best evaluation?
options: It must be correct because oil companies know about fuels.
It must be wrong because it was paid for by a company.
It is more reliable than peer-reviewed work because it is newer.
It may be biased and has not been checked by other experts, so it should be treated with caution.
markScheme: 1 mark: possible bias and not peer reviewed, so treat with caution
questions.explanation: Funding does not automatically make a report wrong, but a possible conflict of interest and lack of peer review reduce confidence.

questions.question:
Methane burns completely in oxygen.
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 1.0 kg of methane burns completely.
Give your answer in kg.
Relative formula masses (Mr): CH₄ = 16   CO₂ = 44
markScheme: 1 mark: moles CH₄ = 1000 ÷ 16 = 62.5 mol
1 mark: moles CO₂ = 62.5 mol (1 : 1 ratio)
1 mark: mass CO₂ = 62.5 × 44 = 2750 g = 2.75 kg
questions.explanation: Converting kg to g first keeps the units consistent with Mr in g/mol. Note that the mass of CO₂ is greater than the mass of fuel because oxygen from the air is added.

questions.question:
A car produces 120 g of carbon dioxide per km.
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced on a journey of 250 km.
Give your answer in kg.
questions.explanation: Multiply the emission per km by the distance, then convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000.

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: burning fossil fuels (accept named fuel or use, for example driving petrol cars, coal power stations)
1 mark: deforestation
questions.explanation: These are the two activities named in the specification for carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase the amount of methane in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: animal farming (cattle/livestock digestion)
1 mark: decomposition of rubbish in landfill sites (accept rice paddy fields)
questions.explanation: Methane comes from digestion in livestock and from decay without oxygen in landfill and waterlogged rice fields.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the complete combustion of methane.
markScheme: 1 mark: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
1 mark: state symbols (g), (g), (g), (l); accept H₂O(g)
questions.explanation: Methane and oxygen are gases; carbon dioxide is a gas; water is liquid at room temperature (or gas at the flame temperature).

questions.question: Explain why the increasing world population has led to more methane in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: more people need more food / produce more waste
1 mark: so more cattle are farmed (or more rice grown, or more rubbish in landfill), which release methane
questions.explanation: Link population to a source of methane: livestock, rice paddies or landfill.

questions.question: Explain why peer review is important for evidence about climate change.
markScheme: 1 mark: other scientists/experts check the methods, data and conclusions
1 mark: so errors or bias are more likely to be found, making the evidence more reliable/trustworthy
questions.explanation: Peer review is a quality check; it does not guarantee results are correct but increases confidence.

questions.question: Suggest three uncertainties in the evidence used to predict future global climate change.
markScheme: 1 mark each for up to three: climate is complex so models are simplified; future human emissions are unknown; natural variation (for example volcanic eruptions, solar changes); effects of clouds or oceans hard to model; past temperature records are limited or indirect
questions.explanation: Describe uncertainties in the evidence base, not reasons why climate change is not happening.

questions.question: Explain why scientists need to communicate their results about climate change to a wide range of audiences.
markScheme: 1 mark: so the public and politicians/decision makers understand the evidence
1 mark: so informed decisions or policies can be made / to counter misleading or biased reports
questions.explanation: Climate decisions are made by governments and individuals, so they need accurate, understandable information.

questions.question: Microorganisms decompose rubbish buried in landfill sites. Explain why this releases methane rather than mainly carbon dioxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: the rubbish is buried so there is little or no oxygen, and decomposition without oxygen produces methane
questions.explanation: When waste decays with plenty of oxygen, carbon dioxide is the main product. Buried waste is cut off from air, so methane is produced instead.

questions.question: Which gas is produced when a fossil fuel burns completely and is a greenhouse gas?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is used up, not produced.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the approximate concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere between 1960 and 2020.
The graph gets steeper between 1960 and 2020.
Suggest two reasons why the rate of increase has gone up.

questions.question: Describe how human activities have increased the amounts of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere.
markScheme: Indicative content: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels (power stations, vehicles, heating), combustion converts carbon in fuels to CO₂; deforestation: trees burned release CO₂ and fewer trees for photosynthesis; methane from animal farming (cattle digestion), landfill (decomposition of rubbish without oxygen), rice paddy fields; increasing population increases these activities.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two activities for each gas, with some explanation of how each releases the gas.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two activities named with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Give two named activities per gas and say how each one produces the gas.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation considering both parts of the claim, using data or named human activities, referring to peer review and to uncertainty in models, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some evaluation of one part of the claim with relevant science, and a conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple agreement or disagreement with limited reasons.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means consider strengths and weaknesses of the claim, then reach a supported conclusion.
